    Profiling a database

    Source: vignettes/articles/profiling-a-database.Rmd
    profiling-a-database.Rmd

    This guide is the English version of 10. Perfilar una base. lupa writes its messages and tables in Spanish, so the output below is in Spanish.

    There is a sales table in a database, perhaps too large for the memory of the session. How is it decided what the engine computes and how many rows reach R, and where is it recorded how they were chosen?

    In this guide:

    • profiling a table with perfilar_dbi() and telling apart its 2 blocks, resumen_tabla and perfil_muestra;
    • comparing what each option brings into R: the default call, muestra = n, universo = "muestra_motor" and bloque_muestra = "solo_agregados";
    • finding the sampling metadata, which lives in 2 places depending on the option;
    • reading the result with the same accessors as a profile in memory.

    A table in a database

    The example uses SQLite in memory, with the packages DBI and RSQLite. The table has 1,000 rows so that the guide runs in seconds; the decisions are the same with millions. DBI::dbWriteTable() only prepares the example. perfilar_dbi() (profile through DBI) sends read queries: it does not write to the database or create temporary tables.

    library(lupa)

n <- 1000
ventas <- data.frame(
  id_venta = seq_len(n),
  sucursal = rep(c("Norte", "Sur", "Este", "Oeste"), length.out = n),
  monto = 100 + (seq_len(n) * 37) %% 800,
  fecha = format(as.Date("2026-01-01") + seq_len(n) %% 180),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ventas$monto[seq(7, n, by = 50)] <- NA
head(ventas, 3)
#>   id_venta sucursal monto      fecha
#> 1        1    Norte   137 2026-01-02
#> 2        2      Sur   174 2026-01-03
#> 3        3     Este   211 2026-01-04
    conexion <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbWriteTable(conexion, "ventas", ventas)

    Profiling with the default values 

    completo <- perfilar_dbi(conexion, "ventas")
completo
#> Perfil DBI de ventas
#> Resumen de tabla completa: 4 columnas sobre 1000 filas
#> Clave primaria: no declara clave (fuente `pragma`).
#> Métricas: calculado 45, no_aplica 15
#> Consultas emitidas: 20 (dialecto limit)
#> Derrame estimado: no se pudo estimar (No se pudo estimar el derrame: la conexión no fue
#> reconocida como PostgreSQL y no hay un `pg_stats` portable.).
#> Derrame: no disponible (El controlador no fue reconocido como PostgreSQL; no se puede
#> consultar una estadística de bloques temporales portable.).
#> Perfil de muestra: 1000 filas, reproducible: FALSE
#> Diagnósticos no evaluados sobre la muestra: 3, en `perfil_muestra$cobertura_diagnosticos`
#> No se imprime ningún valor de celda: están en `resumen_tabla$columnas`.

    The printout shows the 2 blocks:

    • «Resumen de tabla completa» is resumen_tabla (table summary): aggregates that the engine computes in SQL over all the rows.
    • «Perfil de muestra» is perfil_muestra (sample profile): perfilar() run in R on the rows that were read.

    The spill lines only have content in PostgreSQL.

    By default, universo = "tabla_completa" (universe = whole table) and muestra = Inf (sample). That means:

    • the aggregates go through the whole table;
    • lupa also brings into R every row that fits within the read caps. The caps are max_celdas_muestra (1,000,000 cells by default) and max_bytes_muestra (512 MiB).

    With this table, all 1,000 rows fit. The default call is not a cheap sample: it is the whole table, if it fits.

    What each option brings into R

    The other 3 decisions are tried on the same table. The result has one row per option, with:

    • how many rows the SQL summary describes;
    • how many were read into R;
    • in which of the 2 places the sampling metadata was left.
    acotado <- perfilar_dbi(conexion, "ventas", muestra = 200, orden_muestra = "id_venta")
en_motor <- perfilar_dbi(
  conexion, "ventas", universo = "muestra_motor", muestra_motor = 150
)
agregados <- perfilar_dbi(conexion, "ventas", bloque_muestra = "solo_agregados")

que_trae <- function(perfil, opcion) {
  muestreo_sql <- perfil$resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo
  muestreo_r <- perfil$perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo
  data.frame(
    opcion = opcion,
    filas_resumen = if (is.null(muestreo_sql)) {
      n_filas(perfil)
    } else {
      muestreo_sql$filas_obtenidas
    },
    filas_en_r = if (is.null(muestreo_r)) 0 else muestreo_r$filas_obtenidas,
    meta_resumen = !is.null(muestreo_sql),
    meta_lectura = !is.null(muestreo_r)
  )
}

rbind(
  que_trae(completo, "por omisión"),
  que_trae(acotado, "muestra = 200"),
  que_trae(en_motor, "universo = \"muestra_motor\""),
  que_trae(agregados, "bloque_muestra = \"solo_agregados\"")
)
#>                              opcion filas_resumen filas_en_r meta_resumen meta_lectura
#> 1                       por omisión          1000       1000        FALSE         TRUE
#> 2                     muestra = 200          1000        200        FALSE         TRUE
#> 3        universo = "muestra_motor"           150        150         TRUE         TRUE
#> 4 bloque_muestra = "solo_agregados"          1000          0        FALSE        FALSE

    Each row answers a different question (por omisión is the default call):

    • muestra = n bounds the read into R, not the aggregates: the summary still describes the 1,000 rows, and the row-level profile, 200.
    • universo = "muestra_motor" (engine sample) with muestra_motor = n changes the universe of the aggregates. The engine chooses the sample only once and lupa keeps it in a copy in the R session. Everything else is computed on those same rows: summary and profile describe the same 150.
    • bloque_muestra = "solo_agregados" (sample block = aggregates only) brings no rows: perfil_muestra stays NULL and there are only counts and summaries computed in the engine. It works for both universes.

    n_filas() (number of rows) always returns the count of the whole table, also with muestra_motor.

    Where the sampling is written down

    The last 2 columns of the table above say whether each place where the sampling metadata lives exists:

    • meta_resumen looks at resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo;
    • meta_lectura looks at perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo.

    Each one exists under its own condition:

    path describes exists when
    perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo the rows read into R there is a perfil_muestra, with any universe
    resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo the sample chosen by the engine universo = "muestra_motor"; otherwise it is NULL

    For the read into R, the metadata says:

    • how many rows were requested and how many arrived;
    • how many the table has;
    • how they were chosen;
    • whether the choice can be repeated.
    lectura <- acotado$perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo
str(lectura[c(
  "filas_solicitadas", "filas_obtenidas", "filas_totales_fuente", "metodo",
  "reproducible"
)])
#> List of 5
#>  $ filas_solicitadas   : num 200
#>  $ filas_obtenidas     : num 200
#>  $ filas_totales_fuente: num 1000
#>  $ metodo              : chr "primeras_filas_segun_orden"
#>  $ reproducible        : logi TRUE

    reproducible is TRUE because orden_muestra = "id_venta" (sample order) was declared and lupa checked on the whole table that this order is unique. Without a declared order, a LIMIT has no guaranteed order. Then reproducible is FALSE, as in the default call:

    sin_orden <- completo$perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo
sin_orden$reproducible
#> [1] FALSE
writeLines(strwrap(sin_orden$motivo_reproducibilidad, 88))
#> No se declaró `orden_muestra`; SQL no garantiza el orden de las filas.

    For the engine sample, the metadata is in the summary. The method depends on what the engine accepts. lupa first tries the variants of TABLESAMPLE. If none works, it orders by a pseudorandom function with the limit of the dialect, as in SQLite.

    del_motor <- en_motor$resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo
str(del_motor[c("metodo", "tamano_muestra", "fraccion", "universo", "reproducible")])
#> List of 5
#>  $ metodo        : chr "random_limit"
#>  $ tamano_muestra: num 150
#>  $ fraccion      : num 0.15
#>  $ universo      : num 1000
#>  $ reproducible  : logi FALSE

    There universo is the size of the table the sample came from, and fraccion (fraction) the part that was taken. The pseudorandom sample changes on every run, and reproducible says so. Each metric of resumen_tabla$sql also declares its scope: the row count is from the whole table and the rest, from the sample.

    sql <- en_motor$resumen_tabla$sql
sql[sql$columna == "monto", c("columna", "metrica", "estado", "alcance")][1:6, ]
#>    columna        metrica            estado        alcance
#> 3    monto              n         calculado tabla_completa
#> 33   monto      n_validos observado_muestra        muestra
#> 34   monto    n_faltantes observado_muestra        muestra
#> 35   monto prop_faltantes observado_muestra        muestra
#> 36   monto    n_distintos observado_muestra        muestra
#> 37   monto tasa_distintos observado_muestra        muestra

    The status observado_muestra (observed in the sample) warns that the value describes the sample. In particular, n_distintos is the cardinality observed in those 150 rows, not an estimate of the cardinality of the table.

    The 2 blocks, side by side 

    data.frame(
  bloque = c("resumen_tabla", "perfil_muestra"),
  calculado_en = c("el motor", "R"),
  filas = c(n_filas(acotado), n_filas(acotado$perfil_muestra)),
  campos_analiticos = c(
    ncol(acotado$resumen_tabla$columnas) - 1L,
    ncol(acotado$perfil_muestra$columnas) - 1L
  )
)
#>           bloque calculado_en filas campos_analiticos
#> 1  resumen_tabla     el motor  1000                15
#> 2 perfil_muestra            R   200               117

    The summary has 15 analytic fields per column. They are the ones SQL can compute without bringing the data: missing values, distinct values, mode, minimum, maximum, mean, median and standard deviation, among others. The profile of the sample has the 117 of perfilar(), but on the rows that were read. That is why lupa does not mix them. Calling the summary a profile would claim a completeness it does not have; reading the profile as if it were of the whole table, too.

    Reading the result with the accessors

    The accessors of Leer un perfil (Reading a profile, in Spanish) work the same on the result of perfilar_dbi(). columnas() (columns) returns the summary of the engine and hallazgos() (findings), the findings of the sample profile:

    columnas(acotado)[, c("columna", "n", "n_faltantes", "n_distintos", "minimo", "maximo")]
#>    columna    n n_faltantes n_distintos minimo maximo
#> 1 id_venta 1000           0        1000      1   1000
#> 2 sucursal 1000           0           4     NA     NA
#> 3    monto 1000          20         784    100    899
#> 4    fecha 1000           0         180     NA     NA
hallazgos(acotado)[, c("columna", "tipo_hallazgo", "severidad", "n_afectados")]
#>    columna               tipo_hallazgo  severidad n_afectados
#> 1 id_venta       posible_identificador         ok           1
#> 2    fecha           alta_cardinalidad sospechoso           1
#> 3    fecha     tipo_declarado_distinto sospechoso           1
#> 4 sucursal casi_duplicados_vocabulario         ok           0
#> 5    fecha casi_duplicados_vocabulario         ok           0
nrow(sql_perfil(acotado))
#> [1] 60

    The engine counted the 20 missing values of monto in the 1,000 rows. In its 200 rows, the row-level profile found that:

    • fecha is stored as text although it holds dates (tipo_declarado_distinto, declared type differs);
    • almost every row carries a different date (alta_cardinalidad, high cardinality).

    sql_perfil() (SQL profile) returns one row per column and metric, with the query that produced it, its status and its reason.

    When the sample was not requested, the accessors do not make up what is not there:

    • hallazgos() returns an empty table with a warning;
    • cobertura() (coverage) declares the block as no_solicitado (not requested), which is not a failure.
    aviso <- NULL
sin_filas <- withCallingHandlers(
  hallazgos(agregados),
  warning = function(w) {
    aviso <<- conditionMessage(w)
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
nrow(sin_filas)
#> [1] 0
writeLines(strwrap(aviso, 88))
#> Este perfil DBI no solicitó la muestra, así que no hay hallazgos por fila. El resumen
#> por columna sigue disponible en columnas(); el detalle, en cobertura().
cobertura(agregados)[, c("bloque", "elemento", "estado")]
#>           bloque elemento        estado
#> 1 perfil_muestra   ventas no_solicitado

    ⚠️ What the summary does not guarantee

    The aggregates are separate queries, and the table can change between one and the next. The summary declares it:

    completo$resumen_tabla$meta$snapshot
#> [1] FALSE
writeLines(strwrap(completo$resumen_tabla$meta$nota_snapshot, 88))
#> No hubo lectura instantánea: cada agregado se midió en su propio momento y la tabla
#> pudo cambiar entre consultas. La cobertura declara las comparaciones incoherentes entre
#> grupos de consistencia distintos.

    If n_validos and n_distintos come out inconsistent and come from different queries, cobertura() adds an alcance_distinto (different scope) row with the 2 statements. It is evidence that the table changed during the run, not an accusation against the engine.

    Before connecting to another engine

    The engine package and the system library underneath are installed by whoever uses lupa. The error that shows up when one of them is missing rarely says which. requisitos_motor() (engine requirements) says it before connecting:

    requisitos_motor()            # the whole catalog
requisitos_motor("mariadb")   # what MariaDB needs and how to get it

    For each engine it returns:

    • the R package;
    • the system library, with its name in Debian and in Fedora;
    • the way to install it without administrator rights, when there is one;
    • the expected dialect;
    • the testing status of the engine.

    ⏱ For a large table

    Before profiling a table of millions of rows, it pays to look at the plan. plan_perfilado_dbi() (DBI profiling plan) counts the queries and the work that perfilar_dbi() would do with the same arguments, without reading data. The guide Engines and scale gathers what is needed to decide:

    • the cost of each metric and the batches of queries;
    • the cost policy;
    • the memory budgets;
    • the copy of the sample that the session keeps;
    • the dialects;
    • the guarantee of the primary key depending on the engine;
    • the matrix of tested engines.
    DBI::dbDisconnect(conexion)

    Summary

    • perfilar_dbi() returns 2 blocks: resumen_tabla, computed in the engine, and perfil_muestra, computed in R on the rows that were read.
    • By default the aggregates cover the whole table. The row-level profile, also by default, brings every row that fits within the read caps.
    • muestra = n bounds the read into R; universo = "muestra_motor" samples in the engine; bloque_muestra = "solo_agregados" brings no rows.
    • The sampling of what was read is in perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo; the one of the engine, in resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo, only with muestra_motor.
    • meta$snapshot = FALSE: the aggregates are not an instantaneous reading.

    🧭 Next step

    A database is not a table: Colecciones (Collections, in Spanish) profiles several tables at once and looks for the relationships between them.
